Operator
Greetings, and welcome to The Hershey Company's Q2 2023 question and answer session. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I'd now like to turn the call over to your host, Ms. Melissa Poole, Vice President of Investor Relations for The Hershey Company. Thank you. You may begin.
Melissa Poole
VP Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today for The Hershey Company's Q2 2023 earnings Q&A session. I hope everyone has had the chance to read our press release and listen to our prerecorded management remarks, both of which are available on our website. In addition, we have posted a transcript of the prerecorded remarks. At the conclusion of today's live Q&A session, we will also post a transcript and audio replay of this call. Please note that during today's Q&A session, we may make forward-looking statements that are subject to various risks and uncertainties. These statements include expectations and assumptions regarding the company's future operations and financial performance. Actual results could differ materially from those projected. The company undertakes no obligation to update these statements based on subsequent events.
A detailed listing of such risks and uncertainties can be found in today's press release and the company's SEC filings. Finally, please note, we may refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures that we believe will provide useful information for investors. The presentation of this information is not intended to be considered in isolation or as a substitute for the financial information presented in accordance with GAAP. Reconciliations to the GAAP results are included in this morning's press release. Joining me today are Hershey's Chairman and CEO, Michele Buck, and Hershey's Senior Vice President and CFO, Steve Voskuil. With that, I will turn it over to the operator for the first question.
Operator
Thank you. We will now be conducting a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. The confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. One moment, please, while we poll for your questions. Our first questions come from the line of Andrew Lazar with Barclays. Please proceed with your question.
Andrew Lazar
Managing Director, Barclays
Great. Thanks so much, and good morning, everybody.
Melissa Poole
VP Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Andrew Lazar
Managing Director, Barclays
I want to ask a bit about the pricing versus volume commentary regarding the full year sales growth outlook. In the comments, sounds like you expect price to be a bit better in H2 and maybe volume is a bit worse than originally planned. So just two questions on this. First, how do we think about the balance between the two in H2, and could volume be down year-over-year in H2? And then more specifically on volume, is the weaker than anticipated volume fully due to just the new pricing actions, or are you reflecting a tougher consumer or competitive environment in that outlook, or both? Thanks so much.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, I'm happy to take that one, Andrew. Your math is right. That's the way we're looking at it. And the price piece, it really is driven by, or the volume impact really is driven by the extra price impact, as we look at the back half. And as we look at volume in the back half, yes, year-over-year, we expect it to be down, but it really is price driven. There's probably a very small portion attributable to the salty misstep in Q2, but the vast majority is just the reaction to price.
Andrew Lazar
Managing Director, Barclays
Great. Great. Thanks so much. I'll pass it on.
Operator
Thank you. Our next questions come from the line of Bryan Spillane with Bank of America. Please proceed with your question. Bryan, could you check if you're self-muted, please?
Melissa Poole
VP Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
All right, let's come back to Bryan.
Operator
Okay. Our next questions come from the line of Ken Goldman with J.P. Morgan. Please proceed with your questions.
Ken Goldman
Equity Research Analyst, J.P. Morgan
Hi, thanks so much. You know, you've done a great job obviously implementing pricing to offset inflation, but, you know, cocoa and sugar are up a lot more. I know you can't talk about pricing that hasn't been announced to the trade yet, but is it reasonable to think that you're maybe considering another list price increase? And, you know, at what point do you start to ask, how high is too high? How do you think about elasticity in the consumer in that environment? So just wanted to get a sense for, you know, kind of the puts and takes as you think about how to deal with and manage maybe, you know, what continues to be an inflationary environment for you.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Sure. I mean, you're, you're right. Cocoa and sugar are historically high. I think I saw a news article this morning talking about cocoa being at a 12-year high on the New York Exchange. But the good news is, you know, we've got experience managing through commodity rushes up and down. And so as we talked about in the past, as we look at dealing with that, you know, price is a lever, but it's not the only lever. And so we look at driving more productivity, driving efficiency through other parts of the P&L, and, in general, driving revenue management is part of our ongoing strategy. And so all the usual levers will be applied. And as I said, it's not the first time we've had to deal with something like this, so we're pretty good at being able to navigate.
You're right, we're not gonna get more specific than that, at this stage.
Ken Goldman
Equity Research Analyst, J.P. Morgan
Thank you. And then just on the comment about increased competitive, I guess, innovation in confectionery in North America, you know, how...
... how incremental is the innovation that you're seeing? Any real surprises in there versus your prior expectations? You know, it's been such a, I don't want to say benign, competitive environment, because obviously you have some, you know, tough players in the market. But I, is it getting more intense than what you would have expected, I guess, is what I'm going for there?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah. So I would say, you know, the innovation is up off of a relatively low base. So that, you know, it's having an impact based on that. I think, many folks have been focused, certainly we've been focused a lot on execution and meeting demand for the past few years, and focused on the core, with innovation not playing as big of a role. And I think now we're just seeing competitors in the marketplace start to dial up the innovation more back to historic levels. And as we go forward, that's certainly an area that we're going to be focused on as we are continuing to increase capacity, at the same time.
Ken Goldman
Equity Research Analyst, J.P. Morgan
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question has come from the line of Max Gumport with BNP Paribas. Please proceed with your questions.
Max Gumport
Director of Equity Research, BNP Paribas
Hey, thanks for the question. With regard to the increased chocolate capacity this year and the additional co-manufacturing capacity you secured in sweets for next year, is there any way you can help us dimensionalize how sizable those capacity increases are? Just as we try to get a sense for how impactful these additions could be for volumes in the second half and also in 2024. Thank you.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, we're, I think we've said in the past that if you took a look at the capacity that we have coming online this year, that's already gone into place, and then what's coming in the back half, and look kind of year-over-year, you're in somewhere in the 5% range of the incremental capacity across chocolate and sweets.
Max Gumport
Director of Equity Research, BNP Paribas
Great. Thanks very much.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
You bet.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Michael Lavery with Piper Sandler. Please proceed with your questions.
Michael Lavery
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, Piper Sandler
Thank you. Good morning.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Michael Lavery
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, Piper Sandler
You've got the integration in salty snacks and the transition to SAP that you've been talking about, and those never seem to be totally smooth or easy. You mentioned there's some hiccups that you've seen, but can you just maybe give a little sense of what those look like in a little more detail, and specifically with an eye on just having a sense of what's to come? You know, what have you learned and how confident are you that the rest of the year can avoid some of those hiccups or, you know, just be even smoother still?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, I mean, I would say overall, certainly one of our key focuses as we planned for this year, was that at the enterprise level, really focusing on the stellar execution. We planned the business in a way to assume that we would be trying to front load performance, knowing that, you know, there are always hiccups in the execution, and so in Q4, we do expect to see volumes be down, and we put that in our plan. The teams are all over it. It is a focused effort, not just within IT, but across every functional area of the salty business. And so far, we've been, you know, doing pretty well on salty, with household penetration growing, repeat frequency, strong sales.
You know, we did have the promotional shift into Q3, and we feel good about being able to execute that, but we feel like we're well geared up to be able to, to execute that. That said, we certainly do believe that there will be volatility in the back half of the year with the ups and downs of S/4.
Michael Lavery
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, Piper Sandler
Okay, that's helpful. And just back to pricing, yeah, you've got delays in some of the, you know, timing between the announcement and implementation, and then seasons, of course, have a staggered effect. And with just some of the maybe layers to it, can you give a sense of just what you've announced already or put in place already has an impact on 2024? It looks like at least a low single digit, maybe, my math guesses or, you know, estimates close to what, three points you might already have in hand. Is that about right, or what are some of the moving parts, just so we have a little bit further look ahead of what's already put in place?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
So we have high single digits in the second half of this year, and as we look to 2024, low single-digit pricing.
Michael Lavery
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, Piper Sandler
Just to clarify, that's without any other... That would be before there's anything else that might still be to come, right?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
That's what we've announced.
Michael Lavery
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, Piper Sandler
Perfect. Thanks so much.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Pamela Kaufman with Morgan Stanley. Please proceed with your questions.
Pamela Kaufman
Executive Director and Equity Analyst, Morgan Stanley
Good morning.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Pamela Kaufman
Executive Director and Equity Analyst, Morgan Stanley
Your advertising spend was up 15% this quarter, which is an acceleration from Q1. Given the better than expected performance and gross margins for the year and what you're seeing in the competitive and demand environment, are there any changes to your plans for marketing spend for this year relative to before?
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
No, no fundamental changes. So, you know, we had expected this year to be a year to, to invest in brands. And, and again, as we have capacity coming online and, you know, leaning into seasons, especially as we get to the back half, a significant increase in brand investment was planned, and we're executing to that plan.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Also, as mentioned, we were, you know, working to really front load more of our salty planning because of S/4. So, our plans accounted for that as well.
Pamela Kaufman
Executive Director and Equity Analyst, Morgan Stanley
And then just in the prepared remarks, there are comments about some private label launches in your salty snacks categories. I-
... you're generally in categories that face very little private label competition. But considering the launches that you alluded to, just curious to hear how you're thinking about managing private label competition in your categories, and how you're addressing it.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah. So certainly, there is a bit more private label in salty than in CMG. But we've continued to see that while private label has ticked up a bit, our brands have continued to remain quite strong and do incredibly well. And as we look at private label, even within the confection category, while there has been increased activity there, it's remained a very small part of the category, less than 3%, and the entries we've seen in the marketplace this year are still relatively small. So we don't take our leadership for granted. We certainly, you know, continue to invest in our brands to make sure that our propositions are strong, but we feel very well about how we're competing right now in the marketplace on that.
Pamela Kaufman
Executive Director and Equity Analyst, Morgan Stanley
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next questions come from the line of Nik Modi with RBC Capital Markets. Please proceed with your question.
Nik Modi
Managing Director, RBC Capital Markets
Yeah, thank you. Good morning, everyone. Michele, I was-
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Nik Modi
Managing Director, RBC Capital Markets
Good morning. I was hoping you could just kind of address, you know, the Halloween, you know, season as it relates to some of your competitors are still struggling with supply chain and have cut back their orders. And I'm just curious, do you, you know, how can you take advantage of this? Do you have visibility at this point in terms of maybe securing some of that, you know, missed opportunity by, by some of your competitors? Just wanted to get some clarity on how you think about that as it relates to the third quarter.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah. So we are expecting a very strong Halloween. We know that customers are planning big displays, and we are certainly participating in that, and as well have strong marketing support to consumers planned as well. So we have certainly taken an approach of leaning into Halloween. We feel good that there will be plenty of candy out there. So feeling good about that. As we look at overall in the back half as it relates to market share, you know, we think that there'll be a stable approach overall, but, you know, some pressure on everyday, despite some of our strengths around the seasons.
Nik Modi
Managing Director, RBC Capital Markets
Great. And then, if I could just clarify, you know, in terms of the execution issues in salty snacks, what exactly happened? So you talked about systems changeover, but can you just provide us the details on exactly like what the problem was?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, I mean, I'd say two key things. One is we had some promotions that we had planned to occur in Q2 that shifted to Q3, and then we have had some just basic issues as we've been bringing together all of those businesses that you would expect during a transition like that around, sales, commercial, and supply chain execution. So things just weren't as connected as they needed to be. We feel very good that the team is on it and focused on it, and execution is something that we tend to do very well, so we have a lot of confidence in our ability to, to focus and get that back around.
You know, that said, of course, the back half of the year, as we've mentioned, is gonna have a lot of volatility that's really tied to S/4 as we build inventory and then, you know, work through the implementation and anticipate that we'll have later sales in the fourth quarter as a result of that. But we have confidence in our ability to fix the execution.
Nik Modi
Managing Director, RBC Capital Markets
Great. Thanks so much. I'll pass it on.
Operator
Thank you. Our next questions come from the line of Alexia Howard with Bernstein. Please proceed with your questions.
Alexia Howard
Research Analyst, Sanford Bernstein
Good morning, everyone. Can I ask, first of all, about market share trends in US chocolate? It sounds as though capacity constraints and other issues have caused some of those declines. Do you have a view as to when those market share trends should start to improve and turn positive again?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
So we expect to continue to see pressure in the back half of the year. We believe that we'll start to see some improvement, but there are a couple things that are really impacting share. So one certainly is around category mix, with refreshment and sweets being stronger than we had anticipated. Chocolate should improve, and we are focused on, you know, increasing our level of innovation to be even more competitive, and we'll be in a better position to do that as we continue to have more capacity come online.
Alexia Howard
Research Analyst, Sanford Bernstein
Great.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
We've added incremental, yeah, go ahead.
Alexia Howard
Research Analyst, Sanford Bernstein
So I'm sorry. No, I was gonna say, moving on to salty snacks. You talked about a double-digit decline, I think, in the fourth quarter because of the transformation. Is that choppiness expected to persist into 2024?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
No,
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Not, not at this stage. You know, really, it's just the Q3 will be getting ready and building inventory for the switchover. Q4 will be the switchover and the recovery. So by the time we get to the first quarter, we'd expect to be back on a, back or very close to a regular glide path.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah.
Alexia Howard
Research Analyst, Sanford Bernstein
Great. Thank you very much. I'll pass it on.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
You bet.
Operator
Thank you. Our next questions come from the line of Matt Smith with Stifel. Please proceed with your question.
Matthew Smith
Managing Director, Stifel
Hi, good morning. Steve, I wanted to dig in a little bit on gross margin. You had a really solid first half with margin expansion up near a hundred basis points, and you again increased the margin expectations for the year. So could you talk about the drivers of margin expansion relative to your initial expectations and what's weighing on the expansion in the second half relative to the performance in the first half? Is that tougher comparisons in relation to-
... the balance of pricing and inflation, or are there other factors at play, like increased promotion?
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Sure. Yeah, we're pleased with the gross margin performance through the first half. And, you know, we've had a few things, I think, that have broken our way. You know, we've seen less inflation in things like packaging, logistics, and even some material costs. Our productivity progress has been strong. I think, feel really good about where we're at the midyear mark on productivity. And then, of course, we've had, you know, pricing drop through. So all of that, those have worked in our favor and will continue to some degree as we go to the back half. Though, as you look at the back half, you know, taking the, the volume impact, we're gonna have some more fixed cost absorption, impact that will, will be a little bit of a weight.
And again, we've got hedging against commodities, but still from a year-over-year and, you know, beginning of the year, end of year perspective, we still have a bit more cost for some of the inflationary commodities, cocoa and sugar, smaller weights, and again, smoothed out by hedging, but still some impact. Those are probably the two biggest drags as we look to the back half, but again, overall, still feel confident taking our guidance up, and the team's doing a nice job managing the cost side.
Matthew Smith
Managing Director, Stifel
Thank you for that. Just as a follow-up, if I understood what you were saying about the second half, there should be a nice gross margin benefit in the third quarter as you build inventory with retailers ahead of the cutover in salty snacks. Is that, is that right?
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, yeah, we'll get some benefit. Again, salty is not the biggest business, but we will get some absorption benefit as we build inventory in salty. Yep.
Matthew Smith
Managing Director, Stifel
Okay, thank you for that. I'll pass it on.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question has come from the line of Cody Ross with UBS. Please proceed with your questions.
Cody Ross
Lead US Packaged Food Analyst, UBS
Good morning. Thank you for taking our questions. A couple housekeeping ones and then a longer term one in nature. First one, I think you spoke about inventory headwinds in the quarter. I think they were lapping the inventory replenishment last year and the pull forward of sales into Q1 from Q2. Is that correct? And if so, can you quantify each one for us?
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
It is correct. In terms of breaking out the pieces, there's about 300 basis points we attribute to the lap and about 150 basis point shift relative to Q1, you know, order of magnitude.
Cody Ross
Lead US Packaged Food Analyst, UBS
Great. Thank you. Other housekeeping question. Just as far as the Q4, I think you guys said that sales should be down double digits in the salty business due to the ERP implementation. Can you just quantify that for us or give us an expectation for magnitude? And then just one last one.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
In terms of dollars, or?
Cody Ross
Lead US Packaged Food Analyst, UBS
Yeah, the dollars that you're expecting from the implementation.
Melissa Poole
VP Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Yeah, that's-
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
I don't know that we get that specific.
No, it's a double-digit decline, so we're not gonna go any more specific than that.
Cody Ross
Lead US Packaged Food Analyst, UBS
Understood. Then last question, just on the competitive environment. There's been a lot of news in the headlines lately about private label and other branded better competitors becoming more competitive. What are you seeing in a competitive, in the competitive environment? I know you said you've seen branded players pick up more innovation. Besides that, are you seeing any step up in promotions? And what's kind of your expectation going forward? Thank you.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, I mean, I'd say, you know, the categories that we are in have always been very competitive, but the good thing is we have rational competitors. And what we're seeing overall, I'd say, is pretty consistent with what we've seen historically. You know, we have seen some higher levels of innovation as supply chains have gotten stronger and people have been able to support innovation. You know, we have seen some increases in private label, I think, with the economic environment in both confection and in salty. But frankly, the results of those entries have been somewhat mixed, and certainly our brands have held up really well. You know, we continue to focus on driving sustainable, profitable growth.
You know, as it relates to confection and promotional activity, display has always been important for that impulse-driven category, and so we didn't see as much of the change in promotion as perhaps some other categories have seen. So that's been much more stable for us, and we anticipate will continue to going forward. So we'll continue to invest, you know, robustly to drive our brands, with innovation, marketing support, what we think is the right level of promotion.
Cody Ross
Lead US Packaged Food Analyst, UBS
Great. Thank you very much. I'll pass it on.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question has come from the line of Jason English with Goldman Sachs. Please proceed with your questions.
Jason English
Managing Director of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Hey, folks. Good morning. Thanks for swapping me in.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Jason English
Managing Director of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Couple questions. First, on salty snacks, promotion shift, it seems odd. Usually, promotions are locked in well in advance for retailers. So, was this an issue of you actually not having a promotion you were planning for, like a misalignment with your sales and finance functions, or did a retailer actually cancel activity on you?
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Yep.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, retailers did not cancel activity on us, but it was really our choice to move a promotion. So that piece is that. And then relative to our broader execution issues, you know, we had some temporary out of stock. We go to market differently with Dot's than we do with SkinnyPop, and the team quickly adjusted, and we've seen our service levels improve. So we don't expect to see that kind of impact in the second half.
Jason English
Managing Director of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Okay, so you canceled promotional activity on your retailer. Is that because of supply constraints, or, or what, what drove that decision?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
No, we really shifted to invest in a promotion in the third quarter that we thought made a lot of sense in advance of S/4. It was a big opportunity for us.
Jason English
Managing Director of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
... Okay. Switching gears, kind of coming back to Mr. Goldman's line of questioning earlier, and a couple other lines of questioning on competitive activity. Your release has a tremendous amount of focus on market share, and rather than driving category growth. We've seen the category actually weaken quite a bit in recent data. So it's a two-part question. First, what do you attribute the accelerating volume declines in chocolate confection to be driven by?
And second, are you incenting your organization on share, and assuming you are, based on the heavy emphasis in the release of prepared comments, how do you manage the risk of us getting back to where we were five, six, seven years ago, where it was kind of sort of always duking it out, promoting away value in the category, rather than what has been a much more, I would say, constructive, competitive environment we've seen over the last couple of years?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, well, you know, as we look at the category, certainly we've had significant pricing in the category. You know, 20% price and, you know, over time, we should see some moderation, and the volume decline should moderate as well. So certainly price has played a factor. I would say we are always focused on driving the category as well as market share, because being the category leader, we know if we drive the category, we stand to have some of the greatest benefits. So we certainly don't approach this as duking it out, but rather how do we continue to connect with consumers and partner with our retail customers to maximize what's gonna be best to drive the overall business and category.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
We've got a lot more tools, and sophistication today to look at the ROIs for how we're deploying things like promotion. There's no intent to get into an arms race of, you know, bad returning investments like that. We'd love, we wanna win with innovation, which we talked about in the remarks, not just spending.
Melissa Poole
VP Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Yeah, I think, Jason, if it helps a little to, you know, we had the, the past, call it two months or so, multiple price increases, about three different price increases hitting retail at the same time, which is kind of what drove that 20% Michele mentioned. That's kind of some that we were at the tail end of lapping some and some new ones were going in. So we would expect that pricing number to come down, and, with that, the volume declines to moderate as well. So in the next couple of months, we would expect that to normalize a bit.
Jason English
Managing Director of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Okay, and I'm gonna cheat with one quick follow-up related to that question. But to my point, how are you incenting your organization, your sales force in particular? Is market share a component to the bonus, or is it just deliver the revenue?
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, today, market share is not a component of most bonuses. It's about delivering the revenue, but we have other metrics around quality of delivery and how it's delivered and where and-
Melissa Poole
VP Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Sales activity-based margins that-
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Correct
Melissa Poole
VP Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
... you know, enable a balance between sales and profitable sales.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, that's right.
Jason English
Managing Director of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Got it. That, that is helpful. Thank you very much. I'll pass it on.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
You bet.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question has come from the line of Connor Rattigan with Consumer Edge Research. Please proceed with your questions.
Connor Rattigan
Senior Equity Research Analyst and VP of Food, Consumer Edge Research
Good morning, thanks for the question. So I guess, as we think about the price, about the pricing environment and increasing elasticity going forward, should we view some newfound capacity as just meeting existing underlying demand? Or is there maybe an opportunity to allocate some of that newfound capacity to take advantage of some strategic revenue management opportunities, such as package resizing or bar weights to drive net price realization going forward?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, we've been very focused on strategic revenue management and pack price architecture on both confection and the salty categories. You know, I think a few years ago, we talked about evolving our pricing approach from just list pricing to how we look more holistically at strategic pricing. In these categories in particular, it's a big opportunity. You know, we continue to focus there on confection and on salty. It's certainly something that, as we acquired these businesses, was a real underdeveloped area of opportunity.
Connor Rattigan
Senior Equity Research Analyst and VP of Food, Consumer Edge Research
Great. Thank you. I'll pass it on.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question has come from the line of Rob Dickerson with Jefferies. Please proceed with your question.
Rob Dickerson
Managing Director, Jefferies
Great, thanks so much. Just have two questions. I just wanna circle back to the, some of the comments you made, Steve, just on cocoa and sugar inflation. I kind of asked, sounds like, you know, there clearly are, other offsets, besides pricing, that you can enact to kind of help alleviate or let's say, soften some of that pressure over the next, two years, given your hedging schedule. But you know, clearly, the cocoa has also inflated, you know, fairly materially over the past few months.
I'm just curious, like, when I try to combine the comments from the offsets, but then the comments, I think in the, or which put in the prepared remarks about potential more promotional activity next year, then all the pricing you've taken is like, do you, do you feel like you're kind of reaching this point such that, you know, maybe market share is a little softer, maybe that's driven by capacity, capacity is coming online, or maybe you need to promote, but also maybe you kind of have kind of hit certain price points that you have to be, like, very careful with at this point on the everyday side of the business. And maybe you don't really want to take more pricing, but, you know, if you hadn't, you would.
So I'm just trying to get a sense as to, like, why you wouldn't wanna basically take a little bit more given where the input cost complex is? Thanks.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Yeah. I mean, those are all the kind of considerations that we look at when we think about, you know, 2024 and beyond. And again, we look at the whole P&L, we look at market share, we look at what competition is doing, and clearly, we look at commodities and where we think they're headed. And so, I don't wanna get more specific on the construct of the 2024 plan, but, you know, those are the kind of things we'll consider. Again, we've navigated this before. We've got a lot of levers at our disposal. Pricing revenue is just one of those levers. And it'll be interesting to see what happens in the cocoa sugar market. I do think, again, those cases are still a lot of speculation.
And again, our hedging strategy gives us an element of smoothing and protection to a degree there. But we'll be watching to see how these markets hold up, because they are at pretty high levels, atypically, and it's not, you know, driven by fundamentals to a large degree.
Rob Dickerson
Managing Director, Jefferies
Okay, fair enough. And then just quickly, you know, the comment on, you know, Halloween should be very strong. Michele, you said, you know, there'll be plenty of candy. But it sounds like, Halloween seasonal sales expect to be up double-digit. So I'm just curious, you know, like, why do you think Halloween will be so strong this year, number one? And then number two, I think last year you did have some benefit from early shipments. So I just wanna make sure there aren't, like, earlier shipments coming. That's it. Thanks so much.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Sure. So, you know, we get a lot of visibility to the seasons because we plan with customers in advance relative to needing to build inventory for the seasons. So we have a lot of good visibility in terms of what is being bought, and we have very strong programs to drive sell-through, so that gives us a lot of confidence. We know that during, you know, difficult economic times, consumers are particularly interested in enjoying kind of the simple things in life, like these seasons, like Halloween. And so that's another kind of tailwind of focus relative to our conviction and why I think we and our customer partners really wanna lean into Halloween.
Rob Dickerson
Managing Director, Jefferies
Okay. Fair enough. And then on the shipment side, doesn't sound like there's any delta there relative to the year ago?
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
No.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Nope.
Rob Dickerson
Managing Director, Jefferies
All right. Super. Thank you.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
You bet.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question has come from the line of Chris Carey with Wells Fargo Securities. Please proceed with your questions.
Christopher Carey
Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo
Hi, good morning, everyone.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Christopher Carey
Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo
So, just a question, kind of clarification around salty. We, we've seen some, you know, deceleration in consumption, you know, mainly volume in recent scanner data. And I'm just trying to understand, and apologies if this has kind of been addressed, you know, in some form, but just to clarify, you know, was any of that because of lack of supply? Because of a shift in promotional programs? You know, said another way, as supply ramps in Q3, sounds like there's some shift in promotional programs.
Would you expect the consumption trend? You know, I realize what you're saying about your reported results in Q3 and Q4, but would you expect consumption trends to pick up, or is what we're seeing, you know, perhaps more indicative of underlying demand? So I just wanna maybe understand how you think about, you know, the balance of those things.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Yep. So promotional declines did drive that deceleration, and yes, we do expect that to pick up in Q3 going forward.
Christopher Carey
Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo
Okay. That's, that's simple enough. Thanks so much.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question has come from the line of Bryan Spillane with Bank of America. Please proceed with your questions.
Bryan Spillane
Managing Director of Equity Research, Bank of America
Thanks, operator. Hey, good morning, guys.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
Good morning.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Morning.
Bryan Spillane
Managing Director of Equity Research, Bank of America
So two quick ones for me. One, just to follow up on elasticity and another one on capital allocation. So first, on elasticity, Michele, is there any pronounced differences across channels? So I guess small format, immediate consumption versus, you know, large box. Just anything there to call out in terms of where, if there's any differences in terms of elasticity across those channels or consumption occasions?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
I don't think that we've seen anything significant across channels, no.
Bryan Spillane
Managing Director of Equity Research, Bank of America
Okay. Then, Steve, just on capital allocation, noticed the dividend increase of 15%. And that obviously, you know, makes the dividend more competitive, I guess, with interest rates going up. But just, can you remind us, you know, again, as we kind of think over the next couple of years and as capital spending normalizes, and again, you know, assuming that there's not some major, you know, strategic event that would affect the balance sheet, just how you're thinking about capital allocation and returning cash to shareholders going forward? And, you know, again, would it be more dividends? Would share repurchases become more pronounced, please? Just kind of how you're thinking about that, you know, as we think about it over the next couple of years, would be helpful. Thanks.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Sure. Yeah, I'd be happy to. You know, no fundamental changes in our capital allocation philosophy that we talked about back at the investor conference. It is a great dividend increase. You know, when you look at that and you look at our targets for payout ratio and so on, we're still, even with this increase, a little bit behind where we'd like to be and where we've been historically. So, and that just reflects the great earnings progress over the last few years. But pleased with the 15% increase.
You're right, as we look forward, you know, as capital spending moderates off some of the really high spending we've had here recently, you know, we're gonna look for other ways to be thoughtful with the capital, and, and returning cash to shareholders through repurchases, for example, is our stopgap when we don't have better returning alternatives. So, so that's not gonna change.
Bryan Spillane
Managing Director of Equity Research, Bank of America
Okay, thank you.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
You bet.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question has come from the line of Robert Moskow with TD Cowen. Please proceed with your questions.
Robert Moskow
Managing Director, TD Cowen
Hey, thank you for the question. Similar to Brian about elasticity, but slightly different. I wanna know if you, if you've seen any differences in elasticity within the portfolio, like multi-serve bags versus single serve. Especially heading into Halloween, you know, some of those bags can cost $20 to $25 at retail. Have you seen any observations in consumer behavior about just the absolute price points affecting demand?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
So nothing material relative to the pack size piece. I mean, what we have tended to see over time is seasons tend to perform better, to be less elastic, and I think that's just the nature of people are going to participate. So that's the biggest difference that we see.
Robert Moskow
Managing Director, TD Cowen
Okay. So no real change in like single serve demand affected by traffic or just the absolute price point of the bars getting up there?
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
No.
Robert Moskow
Managing Director, TD Cowen
Okay.
Michele Buck
Chairman and CEO, The Hershey Company
I have not seen that.
Robert Moskow
Managing Director, TD Cowen
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question has come from the line of David Palmer with Evercore ISI. Please proceed with your questions.
David Palmer
Senior Managing Director, Evercore ISI
Hi, thanks. At your Analyst Day, you provided guidance of North America confection organic sales in the low single digits, including flattish volume. Could you remind us again of the drivers to sustain that sales growth with low single digit pricing and flat volume, as perhaps competition returns in a more fulsome manner? Thanks so much.
Steve Voskuil
SVP and CFO, The Hershey Company
Yeah, I would say nothing fundamental changing in that algorithm and the way we think about the sources of growth for US confection or the rest of the business. I mean, we always expect it to be a competitive category over time. And so, you know, we're looking at it the same way. There's nothing that's happening, you know, this quarter or even for the balance of this year that we think fundamentally changes any of that.
David Palmer
Senior Managing Director, Evercore ISI
Thanks very much.
Operator
Thank you. I'm showing no further questions in the queue at this time. I'd like to hand the call back over to Ms. Melissa Poole for any closing comments.
Melissa Poole
VP Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Yeah, thanks so much for joining us this morning. I know it was a particularly busy morning of earnings, so thanks for all of the great questions, and look forward to catching up with you all later today for any outstanding ones you may have. Have a great day, everyone.
Operator
Thank you. This does conclude today's teleconference. We appreciate your participation. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Enjoy the rest of your day.

Greetings, and welcome to the Hershey-- to Hershey Company Q1 2022 question and answer session conference. At this time, all participants are on a listen-only mode.... Melissa Poole
Vice President of Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today for The Hershey Company's Q1 2022 earnings Q&A session. I hope everyone has had the chance to read our press release and listen to our pre-recorded management presentation, both of which are available on our website. In addition, we have posted a transcript of the pre-recorded remarks. At the conclusion of today's live Q&A session, we will also post a transcript and audio replay of this call. Please note that during today's Q&A session, we may make forward-looking statements that are subject to various risks and uncertainties. These statements include expectations and assumptions regarding the company's future operations and financial performance. Actual results could differ materially from those projected. The company undertakes no obligation to update these statements based on subsequent events.
A detailed listing of such risks and uncertainties can be found in today's press release and the company's SEC filings. Finally, please note that we may refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures that we believe will provide useful information for investors. The presentation of this information is not intended to be considered in isolation or as a substitute for the financial information presented in accordance with GAAP. Reconciliations to the GAAP results are included in this morning's press release. Joining me today are Hershey's Chairman and CEO, Michele Buck, and Hershey's Senior Vice President and CFO, Steve Voskuil. With that, I will turn it over to the operator for the first question.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, the floor is now open for questions. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. In the interest of time and to allow all participants to ask their questions, we do ask that you please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. You may re-queue for any additional questions that you may have.
Again, that is star one to register questions at this time. The first question is coming from Andrew Lazar of Barclays. Please go ahead. Andrew, your line is live. Please make sure you're not muted on your end.
Andrew Lazar
Senior Director, Barclays
Good morning, everybody. Can you hear me?
Melissa Poole
Vice President of Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Yes, we can hear you.
Operator
Yes, we can.
Andrew Lazar
Senior Director, Barclays
Great, thank you. I guess first off, by our estimate, it seems like you're raising full year organic sales by essentially the over-delivery in the Q1, meaning expectations for the remainder of the year haven't changed. Is that the way you're looking at it? And if so, I guess why is that, given the momentum in the business? And I realize you'll start to lap some of the pricing as the year unfolds.
Melissa Poole
Vice President of Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Hey, Andrew. Good morning.
Andrew Lazar
Senior Director, Barclays
Good morning.
Melissa Poole
Vice President of Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
I'm gonna kick us off with a few responses and ask Steve to jump in as well. So first of all, I'd say we are, you know, we're really pleased with our Q1 results and the momentum that we see on the business. But it is pretty early in the year still, and as we all know, we continue to see significant volatility in the marketplace, you know, whether it's record inflation, the Ukraine-Russia situation, you know, continued disruption in supply chain. As we dissect the business in the Q1, clearly, within the Q1, the large majority of our sales were related to stronger elasticity, you know, that have been realized in the marketplace.
But we do anticipate, as we look further out in the year, that we'll see some moderation on those elasticities, perhaps back to more historic levels.
A lot of that is driven by that reduction in government subsidies and the continued inflation pressure that we think consumers will experience. You know, there was another component of our Q1 sales beat that was about Dot'sand our ability to really get our arms around the Dot's business and better understand what we thought it could deliver for the year. We have pretty good visibility into that. So we feel like the number there is pretty good. And then lastly, as we look at inventory, you know, we've been really working hard to build inventory, and we did get more inventory out to retail. We made a decision to do that in Q1 to really try and increase on-shelf availability.
So from a sales perspective, as we look at what we realized versus what, how we think that will impact back half of the year, you know, we think the strength in Q1 from sales is much stronger. But Steve, do you want to comment more about that and also relative to the cost and profit situation?
Andrew Lazar
Senior Director, Barclays
Yeah, on the top line, I think you hit all the key points. You know, the inventory piece was about a 3-point benefit to the Q1; that'll come out in the back half. So that's one of the unique things I guess, that drove the Q1 performance. And then Michele touched on the elasticities. You know, we saw big benefit in the Q1. We do expect to see elasticities normalize a bit as we go forward, quarter -by -quarter through the year. One thought is, you know, you might layer in as your capacity increases, some more advertising, but some in the industry are talking about digital marketing becoming more expensive and maybe lower ROIs. So just any thoughts on that would be helpful.
Melissa Poole
Vice President of Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Okay. So you know, we are big believers in advertising. I think we've talked a lot about our model is we are pleased to have, you know, some of the strongest gross margins in the industry, and we believe in the model, and then using some of those funds to reinvest in our brands, and be one of the highest investors in the industry. It's a highly responsive category with a strong, you know, impulsive nature as well. As you look to the rest of the year, you know, we believe we will be up mid to high single digits, and we will continue to invest as we expand capacity wherever we can, because we're big believers....
Media efficiencies have really helped us to control the dollar cost because as a result of a new partnership and also new capabilities, we've gotten more efficiencies in our media. I think from a philosophy perspective, relative to your question about digital, we have not seen a decline in lift and return, and I don't know if that's - if they're being offset because we've built capabilities, new capabilities to better target. And so we're actually seeing a stronger targeting capability and, thus, better efficiency. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. At this time, I'd like to turn the call back over to Ms. Poole for closing comments.
Melissa Poole
Vice President of Investor Relations, The Hershey Company
Thank you for joining us this morning. I will be available throughout the day and tomorrow for any follow-up questions you may have. Thank you for your time this morning.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your participation. This concludes today's event. You may disconnect your lines or log off the webcast at this time, and enjoy the rest of your day.
